title: Waterfall
body:
The original [[SDLC]] process model: run each phase once, in order, and do not go back.
Requirements, then design, then implementation, then testing, then maintenance. Each phase
produces a document that the next phase treats as settled.

Its one assumption is the fatal one: that the requirements are correct and complete before
any code is written. That is only true when the problem is genuinely well understood, which
in practice means re-doing something you have built before. When it is wrong, the error is
not discovered until testing, and by then it is buried under every design decision that was
made on top of it. This is the usual illustration of the rule that a defect costs more the
later it is found.

It is not useless. Waterfall is honest about producing documentation, it gives a project a
schedule you can actually track, and it suits contexts where the requirements are fixed by
something outside the project (regulation, hardware, a standard). [[Agile]] is the response
to the case where they are not.

| | Waterfall | [[Agile]] |
|---|---|---|
| Phases | once, in sequence | repeated every iteration |
| Requirements | fixed up front | expected to change |
| Feedback from user | at the end | every cycle |
| Working software | at the end | every cycle |
| Documentation | heavy, phase gates | light |
| Fails when | requirements were wrong | scope has no discipline |

See [[Models]] for where this sits among the process models, and
[[Projects in software engineering]] for the project-management side.
